content.user_title: Manage Azure Durable Task Resources with .NET
content.value_statement: Provisioning Durable Task Scheduler resources through Azure Resource Manager requires precise SDK patterns. This skill provides focused .NET guidance for schedulers, task hubs, retention, updates, and cleanup.
actual_capabilities: Explains package installation and ARM client authentication with DefaultAzureCredential.
Shows how to create Dedicated and Consumption schedulers with idempotent operations.
Demonstrates task hub creation and retention policy management.
Covers listing, retrieving, updating, and deleting scheduler resources.
Provides patterns for long-running operations and common ARM API failures.
Distinguishes management plane resources from data plane orchestration packages.
limitations: It does not start orchestrations, query instances, or run Durable Task workers.
Examples require valid Azure subscriptions, resource groups, RBAC permissions, and environment-specific settings.
It does not deploy, execute, or validate generated workflows automatically.
Package versions and Azure API behavior may change after the documented release.

use_cases.title: Provision a scheduler
use_cases.description: Create a Durable Task Scheduler and task hub with suitable location, SKU, capacity, and network settings.

use_cases.title: Build management tooling
use_cases.description: Add typed C# workflows for listing, retrieving, updating, and deleting Durable Task resources.

use_cases.title: Standardize resource operations
use_cases.description: Define reliable deployment and cleanup procedures with idempotent calls, completion waits, and ARM error handling.

prompt_templates.title: Set up authentication
prompt_templates.prompt: Show how to install the required .NET packages and authenticate an ArmClient with DefaultAzureCredential. Use placeholders for subscription and resource group values.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new management application.

prompt_templates.title: Create a scheduler
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a C# example for a [Dedicated or Consumption] Durable Task Scheduler in [region]. Include a task hub and explain each required setting.
prompt_templates.scenario: Basic resource provisioning with a selected SKU.

prompt_templates.title: Manage the lifecycle
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an idempotent C# workflow that finds, updates, lists, and safely deletes a scheduler named [name]. Handle long-running operations and common ARM errors.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate lifecycle automation for an existing environment.

prompt_templates.title: Design production provisioning
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these workload requirements: [requirements]. Recommend SKU, capacity, IP allowlist, retention, error handling, validation, and cleanup steps for a production-ready management workflow.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced architecture review with operational safeguards.

output_examples.input: Choose a scheduler SKU for a development workload with variable traffic.
output: Recommendation: Consumption SKU for variable development traffic.
Reason: It avoids fixed capacity management and scales automatically.
Validation: Confirm regional availability, quotas, and current Azure pricing before deployment.

output_examples.input: Outline a safe plan to create a Dedicated scheduler and one task hub.
output: Plan: Authenticate, select the subscription and resource group, then create the scheduler with an idempotent operation.
Checks: Verify RBAC, location support, naming, IP allowlist, and operation completion.

output_examples.input: Explain how to investigate an ARM conflict during an update.
output: Diagnosis: The scheduler name may already exist, or another operation may still be updating it.
Next actions: Fetch the current resource, compare desired settings, and use idempotent update logic.

best_practices: Use DefaultAzureCredential and grant only the Azure roles required for each management operation.
Use idempotent operations and wait explicitly when later steps depend on completion.
Validate names, regions, quotas, allowlists, and deletion targets before changing live resources.
anti_patterns: Do not hardcode Azure credentials, subscription identifiers, or production resource names.
Do not use the management SDK for orchestration and worker data plane operations.
Do not delete schedulers before confirming dependent task hubs and the intended environment.

faq.question: Does this skill execute Azure changes?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples. Running generated code with authorized Azure credentials can create, update, or delete resources.

faq.question: Can it start Durable Task orchestrations?
faq.answer: No. Use the Azure Managed Durable Task client and worker packages for data plane orchestration operations.

faq.question: Which authentication approach does it recommend?
faq.answer: It recommends DefaultAzureCredential, which supports local development and managed Azure identities without hardcoded credentials.

faq.question: How should I choose a scheduler SKU?
faq.answer: Use Dedicated for predictable capacity needs. Consider Consumption for variable workloads, after checking availability, quotas, and pricing.

faq.question: What should I verify before deleting a scheduler?
faq.answer: Confirm the subscription, resource group, scheduler name, environment, and dependent task hubs. Ensure recovery or recreation procedures are available.

faq.question: Are the documented package versions guaranteed to be current?
faq.answer: No. Verify package versions, API support, regional availability, and release notes before implementing the examples.
